refusals.why: EV/EBITDA is not applied: no peer in the set produced a meaningful EV/EBITDA, so there is no percentile to apply.

dcf.exit_multiple is unset and no peer in CRWD, MDB, ZS has a meaningful EV/EBITDA to take a median of (CRWD: EBITDA (after operating lease cost, per ASC 842) cannot be formed from this filer's tags; MDB: 3,202x exceeds the 100x cut-off on an EBITDA margin of 0.3%; ZS: 1,626x exceeds the 100x cut-off on an EBITDA margin of 0.5%). The engine does not invent a multiple, so there is no exit-multiple terminal value to draw.

The engine computes two shield conventions, the cost of debt (Modigliani-Miller) and the unlevered cost of equity (Harris-Pringle), and does not compute Miles-Ezzell. Miles-Ezzell discounts each year's shield at the cost of debt for its last year and at Ku before that, which scales the Harris-Pringle value by (1 + Ku) / (1 + Kd). This is a convention the engine does not offer, not a figure the fixtures cannot reproduce, and the page draws only what the engine computes.

engine.takeaway: At the 2026-09-09 close of 225.27, on a 4.83% risk-free rate and a 12.97% WACC, the DCF values DDOG at 31.89 a share on Gordon growth and 28.97 on the value driver, 14% and 13% of the price. No exit-multiple value is drawn; the note under the football field says why. Correlating the simulation's four drivers widens the spread of value by 21%.

fade.takeaway: At one year out the fitted fade ties this year's growth: a mean absolute error of 0.1474 against 0.1510, a lift of +0.0035 inside the fold noise (a mean fold lift of +0.0040 against a fold-to-fold standard deviation of 0.0216). At two and three years it beats persistence by +0.0407 and +0.0530, outside the fold noise. Against the strongest baseline at each horizon the gap is smaller than one fold standard deviation of the model's own error, and from two years out that baseline is the sub-vertical mean. Discounted at 11.28% on its own beta, Datadog is worth 40.61 a share on the fitted path and 36.65 on the typed one.

items.what: Names on the same date are not independent draws
items.why: A hundred names inside one quarter share a sector, a rate cycle and a market, so they are not a hundred draws. The overlap correction deals with dependence through time, between the value signal's 35 rebalance dates, and does nothing about dependence across the names on one date, which nothing in the package corrects.

The SEC's ticker file is today's list and the price sources drop a company the day it stops trading, so every model here is biased by the outcomes it cannot see. It is why the value signal refuses a survivorship correction across its 2,604 company-dates.

items.what: The text corpus is an excerpt
items.why: The committed Item 1 text stops at 2,500 characters, roughly the first two pages of each business description, and the encoder's 0.5407 NDCG@10 is measured on it. What it would score on the full documents cannot be reproduced from this repository.

items.what: There is no market feed in the peer panel
items.why: 14 of the peer panel's 50 features are empty on every row, the market features among them, so the fundamentals tower is judged on a degraded input. Taking that tower out moves the encoder's pair ranking by 0.027, inside a fold standard deviation of 0.086, and that is not a verdict on fundamentals in general.

items.what: The labels are compensation peers, not trading comparables
items.why: A board committee picks a peer group partly for competition over executive talent, and the encoder inherits that choice from the 220 of 320 disclosed groups it can use.

items.what: A warranted multiple cannot say the market is wrong
items.why: It is fitted on the market's own pricing, so a mispricing the whole sector shares is invisible to it by construction. Its residual says where a company sits, not that the gap will close.
The price layer carries closes, so a dividend payer's realised return is understated by its yield. The convention is stated here rather than assumed.

headline.verdict_text: cheapness (negative trailing EV/Revenue): mean IC -0.0984 over 35 dates (2,604 company-dates, about 8 independent 12 month periods). Share of dates positive 43%. t = -2.65 naive, -1.62 Newey-West at lag 3; the correction moved the standard error by 1.64x, leaving about 13 effective observations. The naive statistic clears two and the corrected one does not, so the honest answer is NOT SIGNIFICANT. The naive figure is printed above only so the size of the difference is visible. Top-bottom spread -5.38% over 12 months (t = -0.79), monotone across 25% of the steps. Mean information coefficient of -0.0984 against 0.0002 for a random score with the same cross-sectional shape, 400 permutations within date: the model does NOT beat the baseline on 2,604 observations. Use the baseline.

refusals.why: Not one of the 2,604 holding periods ended at a takeover or a delisting, so the harness had no exit to terminate at a deal or score at a delisting return. Five names in the seed universe (EA, FI, FYBR, IPG, JNPR) have no price rows and no score in the fixtures and are missing from every cross-section. Survivorship is measured here, not corrected. A takeover carries its premium into whichever bucket held the target, so if the missing names skewed cheap their absence biases the coefficient against cheapness, and the true figure is if anything higher than the one shown.

signal.takeaway: Cheapness on trailing EV/Revenue across 98 TMT names predicted 12-month returns with the wrong sign, a mean IC of −0.098 over 35 quarterly dates, and it is not significant once the overlapping windows are corrected: the naive t of −2.65 clears the 5% line, the Newey-West t of −1.62 (p = 0.11) does not.

headline.baseline_name: comps.py OLS refit on the date, sub-vertical peers
headline.verdict_text: Spearman of 0.7651 against 0.6313 for comps.py OLS refit on the date, sub-vertical peers, a lift of +0.1339 on 888 observations. Fold standard deviation 0.0841, so the lift is outside the fold-to-fold noise. 2% of the variance in the log multiple sits between the 22 dates rather than inside them: a model given the date and nothing else scores an R-squared of 0.02 against the raw multiple. That is the re-rating, and it is not a statement about any company. Differenced against each company's own previous observation the rank correlation is +0.0420 on 1,548 observations, so almost all of the score above is the level inherited from history rather than a view about the change. Treat the residual as a description of where a company sits, not as a forecast of where it is going.

refusals.what: Screen of rich and cheap names
refusals.why: None of the screen's 16 names on 2026-06-30 is itself flagged by the enterprise-value audit, but every residual is measured against a model fitted on the whole panel, and on that date the audit flags 5 of the 84 names ranked that day (DLR, EBAY, TMUS, VZ and WBD) and 9 rows today's code would admit and the ranking leaves out (ACN, CMCSA, DXC, LRCX, LUMN, MU, NXPI, PSKY and T). Refitting with only the enterprise values rebuilt, a partial refit that leaves the features as recorded, changes 1 of its 16 names: TXN leaves it and PLTR joins. A screen that calls a company rich or cheap on enterprise values now known to be wrong is not drawn, and re-recording the panel with today's debt ladders is the fix.

warranted.takeaway: The network ranks EV/Revenue multiples better than the strongest peer baseline, comps OLS on sub-vertical peers: 0.7651 against 0.6313 on 888 observations, a lift inside the spread of the per-fold lifts. Differenced against each company's own previous observation it predicts the change at +0.0420 on 1,548, so almost all of the ranking is company identity inherited from history. The panel predates the debt-ladder fix: rebuilt with today's code, 106 of its 1,713 enterprise values move by more than 5%, at 13 filers, so the screen is not drawn and every score here is the panel as recorded.
